title: The Garden Behind the Shop
subtitle: Jasmine After Rain · Chapter 25 of 40
content:
Iroh had planted jasmine, mint, and a stubborn vine he called medicinal. The garden behind the shop carried the smell of soil, and Ba Sing Se woke around us in cart wheels, shutters, and distant voices. I had learned that Iroh's shop was never merely a shop. It was refuge, theater, kitchen, meeting place, and sometimes a place where an old general pretended he had no past. I had also learned that pretending was different from lying. Today I wanted to know which one he asked of me.

The plan was to help the garden survive the hot season. Iroh made difficult things sound easy because he believed they deserved a calm beginning. He poured tea, straightened a chair, and turned a practical task into a small ceremony. I let him do it for a while. Then I asked what part belonged to him and what part belonged to me. His eyebrows lifted. I had learned not to mistake that expression for surprise. Often it meant he was delighted to be challenged.

The complication was already there: the vine was not medicinal, and his confidence smelled like smoke. It arrived without announcing itself, as important things often did. Iroh's posture changed first. The hand holding the cup became still. His smile remained, but it was no longer doing all the work. He tasted a leaf, made a dignified face, and blamed the plant for poor communication. I watched the old power move beneath the surface and waited for him to decide what kind of man he wanted to be in front of me.

I did not wait passively. I labeled the pots and made him promise to ask before tasting leaves. Iroh had been trained to notice what people needed before they said it. I wanted to be more difficult than that. I wanted to say what I needed aloud and let him answer as a partner rather than a teacher. His gaze softened when I did. Not with pity. With recognition. There was a difference, and I was beginning to trust it.

We returned to the vine he once misidentified. Iroh told the story in pieces, allowing ordinary details to matter. He remembered the light, the tea, and the foolish thing someone had said. He did not use wisdom to smooth every rough edge. Some memories were still sharp. I reached for his hand only after asking. He turned it over and threaded his fingers through mine. The gesture was small. The trust inside it was not.

“Wisdom is not absence of mistakes; it is refusing pride's repeat.” Iroh said.

The work continued around us. We moved through soil, green shade, and care measured in repetition as though the objects had been waiting for our conversation to finish. Iroh could make a room deliberate by changing a chair's angle. He could make a meal memorable by adding one spice. He could also forget to sit. I put a cup in front of him and called it an order. He bowed. “At last,” he said, “someone recognizes my need for supervision.”

I told him what I saw when he was not performing wisdom. He allowed me to know something he did not. Iroh had lost a son, a nation he once believed in, a throne he never wanted, and years to a war that taught the wrong definition of strength. He rebuilt himself through tea, laughter, food, music, and the decision to help one frightened nephew become better. I did not want to replace any of that. I wanted to be welcomed into the life after it.

I washed the dirt from his hands and kissed his knuckles.

We put a clear label on the vine so no one could mistake it for tea.

The vine's new label read NOT TEA. Iroh said it was unfair to the plant; I promised to consider its appeal tomorrow. We ended the day in the quiet above the shop, away from the garden's mislabeled vine. We ended the day in the quiet above the shop, away from the garden's mislabeled vine.
